transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-11 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (CTO — Calypso), Leah Kim (Lead ML Eng), Omar Farouk (Head of Reliability), Tanya Brooks (Legal)

Summary: Quick discovery — Calypso currently on OpenAI for text generation and embeddings, exploring move for cost predictability, data control, and performance parity. Main concerns: inference parity (outputs identical enough), runtime compatibility with their vLLM/TGI experiments, security (KMS + VPC), and a clear pilot/benchmark plan.

Topics: Current infra and costs, parity/eval approach, hosting models and tradeoffs (hosted vs dedicated vs private), vLLM/TGI compatibility, security/compliance checklist, next steps and pilot scope.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Diego our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:06] Ravi Patel: Morning, good thanks. We're excited, we've been looking at alternatives to OpenAI for a couple months.
[00:10] Leah Kim: Hi, Leah here. We've been running most user-facing generation on OpenAI gpt-4o-mini and embeddings for retrieval.
[00:16] Diego Alvarez: Nice to meet you. Quick confirm — main drivers here are cost, data control, and eliminating vendor lock?
[00:22] Ravi Patel: Yep. Also, we want the outputs to remain consistent. Our product depends on a certain writing style and behavior; parity is critical.
[00:29] Omar Farouk: And from infra, we care about latency SLAs and ability to run in our VPC eventually. So private deploy is on the table.
[00:37] Tanya Brooks: From legal, we need audit logs and KMS integration, also SOC2 if it's available.
[00:42] Maya Chen: Totally, that's all squarely in Redwood's focus. We'll run through hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs and then map out a benchmark to validate parity and perf.
[00:50] Ravi Patel: One thing — we've experimented with vLLM internally and also tried TGI for some workloads. How compatible is Redwood with those runtimes?
[00:58] Diego Alvarez: Good question. Redwood's serving runtime supports models commonly used with vLLM and TGI — but there are differences. Practically we can serve the same weights, run quantization, manage KV cache, and we surface compatibility notes in the model catalog. That said, edge cases exist around custom kernels and patch-level differences.
[01:15] Leah Kim: When you say "serve the same weights", do you mean we can drop our existing fine-tuned checkpoints in? We have a few LoRA adapters.
[01:22] Diego Alvarez: In most cases yes, adapters like LoRA are supported but we need to validate the checkpoint format. Sometimes conversion is required — we've done many LoRA conversions. We'll want a test checkpoint for the bench.
[01:31] Ravi Patel: Our main worry — dev time. If we have to change model code or retrain parts, that'll blow timeline.
[01:36] Maya Chen: Understood. That's why the pilot is scoped as a parity-eval: narrow, same prompt set, scoring metrics. If conversion is needed we scope it as engineering effort.
[01:44] Omar Farouk: Can we talk latency? Our SLO is median p50 < 220ms on short-chat flows and p95 < 600ms. On OpenAI today p50 is ~180ms for 512-token responses.
[01:55] Diego Alvarez: That's reasonable. On Redwood Hosted with optimized kernels and batching we frequently hit p50 in that band for similar models, but p95 depends on batching and cache hit rate. For dedicated or private, you can tune instance types to get lower p95.
[02:09] Leah Kim: Are you using persistent KV cache for chat? We rely on it to keep long-context threads snappy.
[02:14] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we have prefix/KV caching support. Note sometimes transcripts show as K V cash in older logs — ha — but functionally it's persistent session KV caching and we can pin hot sessions to avoid cold starts.
[02:26] Ravi Patel: About output parity — what's the right eval metric? BLEU? BERTscore? Human review?
[02:33] Maya Chen: Good question. We usually do a mix: exact-token diffs for deterministic tasks, semantic metrics like BERTScore or embedding similarity for style/intent, and a small blinded human eval for subjective quality. We'll propose a scoring rubric in the spec.
[02:46] Leah Kim: We can give you our existing prompt set and a smaller hand-graded subset. That should speed things.
[02:50] Maya Chen: Perfect. Please include both generation and few-shot prompts. Also include cost metrics — per-month token counts and current spend so we can do cost modeling.
[02:59] Ravi Patel: Our account shows around $85k/month on OpenAI incl the embedding-heavy indexing jobs.
[03:05] Diego Alvarez: Ok that helps. We'll run cost projections for hosted vs dedicated reserved capacity vs private. Dedicated typically reduces unit cost but comes with commit.
[03:15] Omar Farouk: For private: are there air-gapped or on-prem options? We have regulators asking about data residency in EU.
[03:22] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem. We have a customer on EU-only private deployment. We also integrate with customer KMS (cloud KMS & HSM in some cases). We'll include compliance notes in the security pack.
[03:34] Tanya Brooks: For contracts, we need SOC2, encryption at rest, and ability to restrict access via SSO/SAML. Also retention policies for logs.
[03:42] Diego Alvarez: We support SSO/SAML and RBAC in the console, and retention controls. We can show audit log samples.
[03:48] Ravi Patel: One practical thing — does Redwood support streaming responses and function/tool calling? We use tool calls to enrich responses from internal APIs.
[03:55] Maya Chen: Yes to both. Streaming, function calling, and structured output are supported in the Hosted API; Dedicated/Private follow the same API surface.
[04:03] Leah Kim: Back to runtime parity: we've seen differences in random seeds and top-p behavior between vLLM and your hosting — small style drifts. How do you recommend getting stable outputs?
[04:12] Diego Alvarez: We suggest locking sampling params, controlling temperature/seed across runs, and running the same tokenizer/version. Sometimes tokenizer mismatches cause tokenization drift — we'll confirm tokenizer binary and BPE ops.
[04:25] Speaker 3: [inaudible]... about throughput — if we batch aggressively will latency spike?
[04:30] Diego Alvarez: Correct, batching trades latency for throughput. Redwood's runtime has continuous batching with per-route latency controls so you can set a latency SLO and we balance batching accordingly.
[04:42] Ravi Patel: For the pilot, what would a minimal scope look like?
[04:45] Maya Chen: Minimal pilot: 1) you provide 100-200 representative prompts (Leah to share), 2) we deploy the closest open model and run parity tests including human spot-checks, 3) perf tests to measure p50/p95 and cost per 1k tokens, 4) conversion path if your LoRA adapters need converting. Expected ~2–3 weeks.
[05:03] Leah Kim: That timeline sounds fine. We have a release window late Nov so aim to decide by early Nov.
[05:09] Maya Chen: Good, so decision horizon: early Nov. Pilot complete by late Oct ideally.
[05:14] Tanya Brooks: Legal will need a data processing addendum (DPA) and specifics on data retention.
[05:19] Maya Chen: We'll include DPA templates and compliance artifacts.
[05:22] Omar Farouk: On ops: how do upgrades and rollouts look? We need canarying and automatic fallback in case a model variant regresses.
[05:30] Diego Alvarez: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B tests, automatic fallback to previous model variants, and per-route tracing so you can pinpoint regressions. We can tie regression alerts to eval sets.
[05:41] Ravi Patel: Pricing — can you ballpark hosted vs dedicated unit cost?
[05:45] Maya Chen: Ballpark: Hosted unit cost will be higher but zero infra management; Dedicated reserved capacity reduces per-token unit cost by ~30–60% depending on commit and model. Private will be similar to dedicated once you include infra ops. We'll give specifics after we see your token counts.
[05:58] Leah Kim: Any gotchas with quantization? We use some int8 models in vLLM to save cost.
[06:03] Diego Alvarez: We support quantized execution paths; some quantization artifacts can affect outputs slightly. We'll surface those differences in the parity report. For mission-critical content you might need a small human-run validation step.
[06:16] Ravi Patel: On integrations: we use S3 for artifacts and internal kafka for eventing. Can Redwood pull from S3 or hook into our event bus?
[06:25] Maya Chen: For Hosted we pull artifacts via secure signed URLs; for Dedicated/Private you can host artifacts in your VPC. We also have webhooks and streaming events for inference tokens to your event bus.
[06:36] Tanya Brooks: On the security docs — will you include third-party audit scopes and subprocessor lists?
[06:41] Maya Chen: Yes, that's part of the security pack I'll send.
[06:44] Diego Alvarez: One more technical note: vLLM/TGI variants sometimes ship different default model config (context window, rotary embeddings). We'll specifically check rotary/rope scaling and context compatibility.
[06:56] Leah Kim: Good call. We had one incident where rope scaling mismatch caused hallucinated tokens.
[07:02] Maya Chen: Okay, action items recap coming. But quick question — do you have a preference between Redwood Hosted (fastest to test) versus Dedicated for the pilot?
[07:10] Ravi Patel: Hosted for pilot sounds easiest; if parity and cost look good we'll talk Dedicated reserve or Private.
[07:16] Omar Farouk: Agree. Hosted for initial bench, then Dedicated for scale if unit cost is favorable.
[07:21] Maya Chen: Great. We'll set up a Hosted pilot cluster and run parity + perf tests.
[07:26] Speaker 3: [crosstalk]... deck link?
[07:28] Maya Chen: I'll drop the pilot spec and our standard deck — here's a link in the calendar notes (https://drive.example.com/redwood-calypso-pilot).
[07:36] Ravi Patel: Perfect. Anything else from legal?
[07:39] Tanya Brooks: No, just waiting for the DPA and SOC2.
[07:42] Maya Chen: We'll include both. Diego, we'll need a benchmark plan and a quick infra checklist.
[07:47] Diego Alvarez: On it — I'll include vLLM/TGI conversion notes and a list of tokenizer checks.
[07:52] Leah Kim: I'll export the prompt set and cost metrics by Tuesday.
[07:56] Maya Chen: Recap and next steps: Maya send security pack + pricing (10/15), Diego send benchmark spec (10/16), Leah provide prompts and token counts (10/13), Omar confirm residency/KMS constraints (10/14), schedule tech deep dive week of 10/19.
[08:14] Ravi Patel: Sounds good. Appreciate the clarity.
[08:17] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
[08:21] Tanya Brooks: Thank you.
[08:23] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-attribution ('K V cash' for KV cache), some inaudible lines, and speaker 3 label where participant name wasn't linked in calendar.
